example: Their stories appear to rupture time, bringing them within a hair's breadth of one another.
correct_substitution: Their stories appear to rupture time, bringing them extremely close to one another.
explanation_correct: A hair's breadth means an extremely small distance, so the stories are brought very close together.
incorrect_substitution: Their stories appear to rupture time, bringing them a vast distance apart from one another.
explanation_incorrect: A hair's breadth means an extremely small distance, but the sentence describes the stories being far apart.

example: 'A little bird told me it was your birthday,' he said.
correct_substitution: 'Someone told me privately it was your birthday,' he said.
explanation_correct: A little bird told me means learning something from a source the speaker won't name, which is how he introduces knowing about the birthday.
incorrect_substitution: 'Everyone announced publicly that it was your birthday,' he said.
explanation_incorrect: A little bird told me means learning something from an unnamed private source, but the sentence describes the news being openly announced.

example: 'Penny for your thoughts,' teased Stephen, coming to put his arms round her waist.
correct_substitution: 'Tell me what you are thinking,' teased Stephen, coming to put his arms round her waist.
explanation_correct: A penny for your thoughts is a gentle way of asking what someone is thinking about.
incorrect_substitution: 'Keep your thoughts to yourself,' teased Stephen, coming to put his arms round her waist.
explanation_incorrect: The phrase invites someone to share their thoughts, but the sentence tells her to stay silent.

example: Chris Howes spends a pretty penny, with no regrets.
correct_substitution: Chris Howes spends a considerable sum of money, with no regrets.
explanation_correct: A pretty penny means a substantial amount of money, describing his spending.
incorrect_substitution: Chris Howes spends a negligible sum of money, with no regrets.
explanation_incorrect: A pretty penny means a large sum, but the sentence describes trivial spending, which would not need excusing.

example: In the penalty box he is above par.
correct_substitution: In the penalty box he performs better than the usual standard.
explanation_correct: Above par means exceeding the normal expected level of performance.
incorrect_substitution: In the penalty box he performs worse than the usual standard.
explanation_incorrect: Above par means exceeding the standard, but the sentence describes falling below it.

example: An election could come at any time, and policies across the board were being honed in readiness.
correct_substitution: An election could come at any time, and policies in every area were being honed in readiness.
explanation_correct: Across the board means applying to everything equally, so all policy areas were being prepared.
incorrect_substitution: An election could come at any time, and policies in one narrow area were being honed in readiness.
explanation_incorrect: Across the board means applying to everything equally, but the sentence limits the work to a single narrow area.

example: A factor which could be regarded as an act of God now intervened.
correct_substitution: A factor which could be regarded as an uncontrollable natural event now intervened.
explanation_correct: An act of God refers to a natural event outside human control, which is how the intervening factor is characterised.
incorrect_substitution: A factor which could be regarded as a deliberate human decision now intervened.
explanation_incorrect: An act of God refers to an event beyond human control, but the sentence attributes it to a person's choice.

example: MIPS' poor first quarter figures — see page three — will only add fuel to these fires.
correct_substitution: MIPS' poor first quarter figures — see page three — will only make an already bad situation worse.
explanation_correct: To add fuel to the fire means to worsen an existing bad situation, which is what the poor figures will do.
incorrect_substitution: MIPS' poor first quarter figures — see page three — will only calm an already tense situation.
explanation_incorrect: To add fuel to the fire means to worsen a bad situation, but the sentence describes the figures easing tensions.

example: Although she understood why he wanted her to bend the truth, it still went against the grain.
correct_substitution: Although she understood why he wanted her to bend the truth, it still conflicted with her natural instincts.
explanation_correct: To go against the grain means to conflict with someone's natural inclination, which is why she resisted despite understanding.
incorrect_substitution: Although she understood why he wanted her to bend the truth, it still felt entirely natural to her.
explanation_incorrect: To go against the grain means to conflict with one's natural inclination, but the sentence describes it feeling completely natural.

example: This strategy needs to be inverted — and Greece offers a real opportunity to get ahead of the curve.
correct_substitution: This strategy needs to be inverted — and Greece offers a real opportunity to act before events demand it.
explanation_correct: Ahead of the curve means anticipating developments rather than reacting to them.
incorrect_substitution: This strategy needs to be inverted — and Greece offers a real opportunity to act long after events demand it.
explanation_incorrect: The idiom means anticipating events, but the sentence describes lagging behind them.

correct_substitution: So stay in a position of advantage over your rivals and don't miss TODAY tomorrow and every Saturday.
explanation_correct: Ahead of the game means being in a better position than competitors, which is what readers are urged to maintain.
incorrect_substitution: So stay trailing well behind your rivals and don't miss TODAY tomorrow and every Saturday.
explanation_incorrect: Ahead of the game means holding an advantage, but the sentence describes lagging behind others.

example: The beast was still very much alive and kicking.
correct_substitution: The beast was still very much active and full of life.
explanation_correct: Alive and kicking means still vigorous and active, describing the beast.
incorrect_substitution: The beast was still very much lifeless and inert.
explanation_incorrect: The idiom means being vigorous, but the sentence describes something without life.

example: JB: I painted mostly in my own time, and it's been like that all along.
correct_substitution: JB: I painted mostly in my own time, and it's been like that from the very beginning.
explanation_correct: All along means from the start and continuing throughout, describing how long the arrangement has held.
incorrect_substitution: JB: I painted mostly in my own time, and it's been like that only since last month.
explanation_incorrect: All along means from the very beginning, but the sentence limits the arrangement to a recent period.

example: When I deciphered one I would announce it to all and sundry.
correct_substitution: When I deciphered one I would announce it to everyone without distinction.
explanation_correct: All and sundry means everyone without exception, so the announcement was made to anyone at all.
incorrect_substitution: When I deciphered one I would announce it to a select few trusted friends.
explanation_incorrect: All and sundry means everyone without exception, but the sentence describes telling only a small chosen group.

example: In that case, they say, all bets are off for co-operation on the budget next year.
correct_substitution: In that case, they say, all previous expectations are void for co-operation on the budget next year.
explanation_correct: All bets are off means prior assumptions no longer hold because circumstances have changed.
incorrect_substitution: In that case, they say, all previous expectations hold firm for co-operation on the budget next year.
explanation_incorrect: All bets are off means expectations no longer apply, but the sentence keeps them in force.

example: A sparrow hawk appeared — and all hell broke loose!
correct_substitution: A sparrow hawk appeared — and sudden chaos erupted!
explanation_correct: All hell broke loose means that sudden uproar and chaos began, which is what the hawk's arrival caused.
incorrect_substitution: A sparrow hawk appeared — and a deep calm settled over everything!
explanation_incorrect: All hell broke loose means sudden chaos erupted, but the sentence describes everything becoming peaceful.

example: Tod also played it cool: all in a day's work.
correct_substitution: Tod also played it cool: an entirely ordinary part of the job.
explanation_correct: All in a day's work means something is a routine part of one's normal duties, so Tod treated it as unremarkable.
incorrect_substitution: Tod also played it cool: an extraordinary feat far beyond anything expected of him.
explanation_incorrect: All in a day's work means something is routine, but the sentence presents it as an exceptional achievement.

example: Swindon probably felt it was all over bar the shouting.
correct_substitution: Swindon probably felt the outcome was already effectively decided.
explanation_correct: All over bar the shouting means the result is settled even though it isn't formally finished, which is what Swindon assumed.
incorrect_substitution: Swindon probably felt the outcome was still completely open.
explanation_incorrect: All over bar the shouting means the result is effectively settled, but the sentence describes the outcome as undecided.

example: Like all children, his mind jumps all over the place.
correct_substitution: Like all children, his mind jumps from one thing to another without order.
explanation_correct: All over the place means disorganised and scattered, describing how his thoughts move erratically.
incorrect_substitution: Like all children, his mind jumps in a careful and orderly sequence.
explanation_incorrect: All over the place means scattered and disorganised, but the sentence describes orderly, methodical movement.

example: With skating there's no-one saying do this, do that all over the shop.
correct_substitution: With skating there's no-one saying do this, do that in a disorganised way.
explanation_correct: All over the shop means done in a chaotic, disorganised manner, describing the absence of scattered instructions.
incorrect_substitution: With skating there's no-one saying do this, do that in a strictly methodical way.
explanation_incorrect: All over the shop means chaotic and disorganised, but the sentence describes rigid orderliness.

example: Well that used to be all the rage once, didn't it?
correct_substitution: Well that used to be extremely fashionable once, didn't it?
explanation_correct: All the rage means being very popular or fashionable for a period, describing its former standing.
incorrect_substitution: Well that used to be widely ignored once, didn't it?
explanation_incorrect: All the rage means being very popular, but the sentence describes it attracting no interest.

example: All other things being equal, the most direct route is the best.
correct_substitution: Assuming no other factors differ, the most direct route is the best.
explanation_correct: All things being equal means setting aside any other differences, which is the condition under which the direct route wins.
incorrect_substitution: Given how sharply the other factors differ, the most direct route is the best.
explanation_incorrect: All things being equal assumes other factors are held constant, but the sentence emphasises that they vary widely.

example: To begin with, you'll find food from the world's four corners and then some.
correct_substitution: To begin with, you'll find food from the world's four corners and considerably more besides.
explanation_correct: And then some means even more than what was just stated, adding to the range of food described.
incorrect_substitution: To begin with, you'll find food from the world's four corners, and that is the full extent of it.
explanation_incorrect: And then some means there is more beyond what was stated, but the sentence presents the list as complete.

example: What really happened is anyone's guess but afterwards each accused the other of cheating.
correct_substitution: What really happened is impossible for anyone to know for certain but afterwards each accused the other of cheating.
explanation_correct: Anyone's guess means that nobody knows the answer, so the true events remain uncertain.
incorrect_substitution: What really happened is a matter of established record but afterwards each accused the other of cheating.
explanation_incorrect: Anyone's guess means nobody knows the answer, but the sentence presents the events as firmly documented.

example: Anything going on in the outdoors which interests, irritates or simply makes you laugh?
correct_substitution: Anything happening in the outdoors which interests, irritates or simply makes you laugh?
explanation_correct: Here the phrase is used literally to mean any occurrence, matching the sense of things happening outdoors.
incorrect_substitution: Only strictly permitted activities in the outdoors which interest, irritate or simply make you laugh?
explanation_incorrect: Anything goes means that no restrictions apply, but the sentence describes a tightly limited set of activities.

example: You're arguing the toss over the small print as to whether or not it's covered.
correct_substitution: You're disputing at tedious length over the small print as to whether or not it's covered.
explanation_correct: To argue the toss means to dispute a decision at wearying length, describing the quarrel over the small print.
incorrect_substitution: You're accepting without complaint the small print as to whether or not it's covered.
explanation_incorrect: To argue the toss means disputing something at length, but the sentence describes ready acceptance.

example: Around the campfire crouched three red-bearded highlanders, clad in musty tartan and armed to the teeth.
correct_substitution: Around the campfire crouched three red-bearded highlanders, clad in musty tartan and carrying every possible weapon.
explanation_correct: Armed to the teeth means heavily and completely armed, describing the highlanders.
incorrect_substitution: Around the campfire crouched three red-bearded highlanders, clad in musty tartan and carrying no weapons at all.
explanation_incorrect: The idiom means heavily armed, but the sentence describes them unarmed.

example: Harriers take off around the clock from hastily constructed hides.
correct_substitution: Harriers take off at all hours of the day and night from hastily constructed hides.
explanation_correct: Around the clock means continuously through the entire day and night, describing the constant departures.
incorrect_substitution: Harriers take off during a brief window each morning from hastily constructed hides.
explanation_incorrect: Around the clock means continuously day and night, but the sentence confines the departures to a short daily period.

example: He didn't as a rule greet all his guests, but this was different.

incorrect_substitution: He didn't on that one isolated occasion greet all his guests, but this was different.
explanation_incorrect: As a rule describes what is generally true over time, but the sentence refers only to a single occasion.

example: Then they magically reappear, leaving your T-shirt looking as good as new!
correct_substitution: Then they magically reappear, leaving your T-shirt looking completely restored to its original condition!
explanation_correct: As good as new means restored to original condition, describing the T-shirt's appearance afterwards.
incorrect_substitution: Then they magically reappear, leaving your T-shirt looking worn and badly faded!
explanation_incorrect: As good as new means restored to original condition, but the sentence describes the shirt looking damaged.

example: As luck would have it a fellow pupil in Diana's dormitory complained that she had appendicitis.

explanation_correct: As luck would have it means something happened by chance in a fortunate way, introducing the coincidence.
incorrect_substitution: According to a carefully arranged plan a fellow pupil in Diana's dormitory complained that she had appendicitis.
explanation_incorrect: As luck would have it means an event occurred by chance, but the sentence presents it as deliberately organised.

example: She could have asked for the moon, and seen the clansmen climb on each other's shoulders to reach it down for her.
correct_substitution: She could have demanded the impossible, and seen the clansmen climb on each other's shoulders to reach it down for her.
explanation_correct: To ask for the moon means to request something unattainable, which the clansmen would still attempt.
incorrect_substitution: She could have demanded the entirely trivial, and seen the clansmen climb on each other's shoulders to reach it down for her.
explanation_incorrect: The idiom means requesting the impossible, but the sentence makes it trivial, which removes the point of the effort.

example: I reckon the teacher fell asleep at the wheel.

explanation_incorrect: The idiom means being inattentive, but the sentence describes close attention.

example: 'At a loose end, Deveraugh?' she queried disdainfully as he followed her out of the tent.

explanation_incorrect: At a loose end means having nothing to do, but the sentence describes him being fully occupied.

incorrect_substitution: One is richly supplied with words to express adequately how one really feels inside, you know.
explanation_incorrect: At a loss for words means being unable to find anything to say, but the sentence describes having ample words available.

example: At a pinch the spacers can be substituted for four appropriately sized nuts.

explanation_incorrect: At a pinch means something done only when necessary, but the sentence presents it as the preferred option.

example: It was ten minutes before she returned at a snail's pace with four rum punches.

explanation_incorrect: At a snail's pace means moving very slowly, but the sentence describes her hurrying.

example: He was used to paddling it for miles at a stretch.

explanation_incorrect: At a stretch means continuously without interruption, but the sentence describes regular breaks.

example: I wouldn't want us to find ourselves talking at cross-purposes.

explanation_incorrect: At cross purposes means misunderstanding one another, but the sentence describes complete agreement.

example: The prospect of an interesting friendship had been destroyed and now they were at daggers drawn.

explanation_incorrect: At daggers drawn means open hostility, but the sentence describes warmth and affection between them.

example: She was a cantankerous woman, but she was literally at death's door.

explanation_incorrect: At death's door means being near death, but the sentence describes her being perfectly healthy.

example: NEW YORK – The world is at a crossroads.

example: But performances have been consistently below par for too long and drastic action needs to be taken.

example: It was sealed with Sellotape and staples, a real belt and braces job.

example: She regularly bent Minton's ear with her problems and he in turn did take-offs of her doing this.

example: You are beside yourself! he uttered, stepping involuntarily backwards.

idiom: between a rock and a hard place

explanation_incorrect: Between a rock and a hard place means being stuck between two bad choices, but the sentence describes both options as attractive.

example: The big hitters were content to wait until 1996.

explanation_correct: A big hitter means a person or organisation of major influence.
incorrect_substitution: The most insignificant players were content to wait until 1996.
explanation_incorrect: A big hitter means someone influential, but the sentence describes minor figures.

example: She's told them what to do, birds of a feather.

explanation_correct: Birds of a feather refers to people who are alike and naturally group together, characterising her and the others.
incorrect_substitution: She's told them what to do, people of utterly opposite character.
explanation_incorrect: Birds of a feather refers to people who resemble one another, but the sentence describes them as completely dissimilar.

idiom: bite off more than you can chew
example: There's always the danger of biting off more than you can chew.

example: Not two minutes in his company and she was biting his head off.
correct_substitution: Not two minutes in his company and she was snapping at him angrily.
explanation_correct: To bite someone's head off means to respond with sudden sharp anger, describing how quickly she turned on him.
incorrect_substitution: Not two minutes in his company and she was speaking to him with gentle patience.
explanation_incorrect: To bite someone's head off means responding with sharp anger, but the sentence describes a calm and gentle manner.

example: Shouldn't we bite the bullet now and legislate, as many are suggesting?
correct_substitution: Shouldn't we face the unpleasant task now and legislate, as many are suggesting?
explanation_correct: To bite the bullet means to force yourself to do something difficult you have been avoiding, which legislating would mean.
incorrect_substitution: Shouldn't we keep postponing the unpleasant task and legislate, as many are suggesting?
explanation_incorrect: To bite the bullet means facing a difficult task head on, but the sentence describes continued delay.

example: You're not meant to bite your tongue like that.
correct_substitution: You're not meant to hold back what you want to say like that.
explanation_correct: To bite your tongue means to stop yourself from speaking, which is the behaviour being commented on.
incorrect_substitution: You're not meant to blurt out everything you think like that.
explanation_incorrect: To bite your tongue means staying silent, but the sentence describes speaking freely.

example: No it's not full, it was just bits and bobs.
correct_substitution: No it's not full, it was just assorted small odds and ends.
explanation_correct: Bits and bobs means a miscellaneous assortment of small items, explaining why the container was not full.
incorrect_substitution: No it's not full, it was just a few large bulky items.
explanation_incorrect: Bits and bobs means small miscellaneous items, but the sentence describes large bulky objects.

example: When Clark took off his shirt he had black-and-blue bruises over his shoulders and arm.
correct_substitution: When Clark took off his shirt he had severely discoloured bruises over his shoulders and arm.
explanation_correct: Black and blue describes skin badly bruised and discoloured, matching the marks on his shoulders.
incorrect_substitution: When Clark took off his shirt he had faint and barely visible bruises over his shoulders and arm.
explanation_incorrect: Black and blue means severely bruised, but the sentence describes marks that are hardly noticeable.

example: Elise had blazed a talented trail to an art college four years before Merrill took up secretarial training.
correct_substitution: Elise had been the first to make a talented path to an art college four years before Merrill took up secretarial training.
explanation_correct: To blaze a trail means to be the first to do something, opening the way for others, which is Elise's role here.
incorrect_substitution: Elise had followed a well-worn talented path to an art college four years before Merrill took up secretarial training.
explanation_incorrect: To blaze a trail means being first, but the sentence describes following a route others had already established.

example: GIANT-KILLERS Yeovil became the most successful non-League club in FA Cup history in this blood and guts seven-goal thriller.
correct_substitution: GIANT-KILLERS Yeovil became the most successful non-League club in FA Cup history in this fiercely committed seven-goal thriller.
explanation_correct: Blood and guts describes a contest fought with raw determination, matching a seven-goal thriller.
incorrect_substitution: GIANT-KILLERS Yeovil became the most successful non-League club in FA Cup history in this tame and bloodless seven-goal thriller.
explanation_incorrect: Blood and guts means fierce commitment, but the sentence describes a lifeless match, which no thriller would be.

example: Meredith told him twice to give it a bit more blood and thunder, but it wasn't in him.
correct_substitution: Meredith told him twice to give it a bit more dramatic force, but it wasn't in him.
explanation_correct: Blood and thunder means violent, melodramatic energy in a performance, which Meredith wanted more of.
incorrect_substitution: Meredith told him twice to give it a bit more quiet restraint, but it wasn't in him.
explanation_incorrect: Blood and thunder means loud dramatic energy, but the sentence asks for subdued delivery instead.

example: 'Blood is thicker than water,' he had replied.
correct_substitution: 'Family loyalty outweighs all other bonds,' he had replied.
explanation_correct: Blood is thicker than water means family ties matter more than other relationships, which is the point he is making.
incorrect_substitution: 'Friendship matters far more than any family tie,' he had replied.
explanation_incorrect: Blood is thicker than water means family bonds take priority, but the sentence ranks friendship above family.

example: 'I blew every gasket in my head!' he admitted deeply.
correct_substitution: 'I lost my temper completely!' he admitted deeply.
explanation_correct: To blow a gasket means to lose one's temper violently, which is what he is admitting to.
incorrect_substitution: 'I stayed perfectly composed throughout!' he admitted deeply.
explanation_incorrect: To blow a gasket means losing your temper, but the sentence describes remaining calm.

example: Yes, so sometimes it has a tendency to seem like you're blowing hot and cold.
correct_substitution: Yes, so sometimes it has a tendency to seem like you're constantly changing your attitude.
explanation_correct: To blow hot and cold means to alternate between enthusiasm and indifference, which is how the behaviour appears.
incorrect_substitution: Yes, so sometimes it has a tendency to seem like you're holding a perfectly steady attitude.
explanation_incorrect: To blow hot and cold means alternating unpredictably, but the sentence describes unwavering consistency.

example: If this has blown my cover, you may not hear from me again.
correct_substitution: If this has exposed my secret identity, you may not hear from me again.
explanation_correct: To blow someone's cover means to reveal their concealed identity, which would explain the danger he faces.
incorrect_substitution: If this has further concealed my secret identity, you may not hear from me again.
explanation_incorrect: To blow someone's cover means revealing a hidden identity, but the sentence describes it being hidden more deeply.

example: Even the pop posters were old, they blew my mind with boredom.
correct_substitution: Even the pop posters were old, they overwhelmed me with boredom.
explanation_correct: To blow someone's mind means to overwhelm or astonish them, here applied ironically to boredom.
incorrect_substitution: Even the pop posters were old, they left me entirely unaffected by boredom.
explanation_incorrect: To blow someone's mind means overwhelming them, but the sentence describes having no effect at all.

example: You can say: the sea was like blue glass, the sand like fine powder, and Bob's your uncle.
correct_substitution: You can say: the sea was like blue glass, the sand like fine powder, and there you have it.
explanation_correct: Bob's your uncle marks a result achieved simply and without further effort.
incorrect_substitution: You can say: the sea was like blue glass, the sand like fine powder, and much hard work remains.
explanation_incorrect: The phrase signals easy completion, but the sentence describes unfinished labour.

example: The use of her own words against her was a body blow and she looked away.
correct_substitution: The use of her own words against her was a devastating setback and she looked away.
explanation_correct: A body blow is a severe shock or setback, describing the effect of hearing her own words turned against her.
incorrect_substitution: The use of her own words against her was a minor irritation and she looked away.
explanation_incorrect: A body blow is a severe blow, but the sentence reduces it to a trivial annoyance.

example: He had been born and bred on the river, but had never seen anything like it before.
correct_substitution: He had been born and raised entirely on the river, but had never seen anything like it before.
explanation_correct: Born and bred means born and brought up in a particular place, describing his lifelong connection to the river.
incorrect_substitution: He had been a recent arrival to the river, but had never seen anything like it before.
explanation_incorrect: Born and bred means having lived somewhere since birth, but the sentence describes him as a newcomer.

example: Come, come, my lords! he murmured, bowing and scraping before us.
correct_substitution: Come, come, my lords! he murmured, behaving with excessive deference before us.
explanation_correct: To bow and scrape means to show exaggerated, servile politeness.
incorrect_substitution: Come, come, my lords! he murmured, behaving with open contempt before us.
explanation_incorrect: The idiom means excessive deference, but the sentence describes disrespect.

example: I can tell you the boys in blue are pleased you've turned up.
correct_substitution: I can tell you the police are pleased you've turned up.
explanation_correct: The boys in blue is an informal term for the police, referring to those glad of his arrival.
incorrect_substitution: I can tell you the local shopkeepers are pleased you've turned up.
explanation_incorrect: The boys in blue refers to the police, but the sentence substitutes an unrelated group.

example: That, and a few water spouts, but then boys will be boys.
correct_substitution: That, and a few water spouts, but then boisterous behaviour is only to be expected of them.
explanation_correct: Boys will be boys excuses rowdy behaviour as natural and unsurprising.
incorrect_substitution: That, and a few water spouts, but then such behaviour is utterly unheard of from them.
explanation_incorrect: The phrase treats the behaviour as expected, but the sentence calls it unprecedented.

example: That certainly qualifies him for a prize for brass neck.
correct_substitution: That certainly qualifies him for a prize for shameless nerve.
explanation_correct: Brass neck means bold, shameless cheek, which is what he is being sarcastically credited with.
incorrect_substitution: That certainly qualifies him for a prize for timid modesty.
explanation_incorrect: Brass neck means shameless boldness, but the sentence describes shyness and restraint.

example: So with football and politics as the bread and circuses of our decadent empire — whither religion?
correct_substitution: So with football and politics as the cheap distractions of our decadent empire — whither religion?
explanation_correct: Bread and circuses refers to superficial entertainment used to keep a population content and unquestioning.
incorrect_substitution: So with football and politics as the demanding civic duties of our decadent empire — whither religion?
explanation_incorrect: Bread and circuses means shallow distraction, but the sentence describes serious obligations instead.

example: Nobody was looking at the thicket at the moment the wounded cow broke cover.
correct_substitution: Nobody was looking at the thicket at the moment the wounded cow emerged from hiding.
explanation_correct: To break cover means to leave a place of concealment, which is what the cow did at that moment.
incorrect_substitution: Nobody was looking at the thicket at the moment the wounded cow settled deeper into hiding.
explanation_incorrect: To break cover means coming out of hiding, but the sentence describes the cow concealing itself further.

example: Any gang member who regularly fails to break even or achieve a surplus would be laid off.
correct_substitution: Any gang member who regularly fails to cover his costs exactly or achieve a surplus would be laid off.
explanation_correct: To break even means to take in exactly as much as was spent, with neither profit nor loss, the minimum standard here.
incorrect_substitution: Any gang member who regularly fails to make a large profit or achieve a surplus would be laid off.
explanation_incorrect: To break even means merely covering costs, but the sentence raises the bar to substantial profit, making the mention of a surplus redundant.

example: Although overdue, two elements of the bill can properly claim to be breaking new ground.
correct_substitution: Although overdue, two elements of the bill can properly claim to be doing something entirely unprecedented.
explanation_correct: To break new ground means to do something never done before, which is the claim made for the bill.
incorrect_substitution: Although overdue, two elements of the bill can properly claim to be repeating well-established practice.
explanation_incorrect: To break new ground means doing something unprecedented, but the sentence describes familiar practice being repeated.

example: Some officers broke ranks and were met with a volley of stones.
correct_substitution: Some officers abandoned the agreed formation and were met with a volley of stones.
explanation_correct: To break ranks means to leave the ordered line or depart from a group's agreed position, which is what the officers did.
incorrect_substitution: Some officers held the agreed formation tightly and were met with a volley of stones.
explanation_incorrect: To break ranks means departing from the group's formation, but the sentence describes the officers maintaining it.

example: For this surely would have broken his heart — he loved us so much.
correct_substitution: For this surely would have caused him overwhelming grief — he loved us so much.
explanation_correct: To break someone's heart means to cause them deep emotional pain, which follows from how much he loved them.
incorrect_substitution: For this surely would have left him entirely unmoved — he loved us so much.
explanation_incorrect: To break someone's heart means causing deep grief, but the sentence describes indifference, which sits oddly with his love.

example: Pouring over its latest simulation runs, Sun is confident it has broken the back of the technical problem.
correct_substitution: Pouring over its latest simulation runs, Sun is confident it has overcome the hardest part of the technical problem.
explanation_correct: To break the back of something means to complete its most difficult portion, which is Sun's claim.
incorrect_substitution: Pouring over its latest simulation runs, Sun is confident it has barely started on the technical problem.
explanation_incorrect: To break the back of something means finishing the hardest part, but the sentence describes hardly having begun, conflicting with the confidence expressed.

example: He doesn't have to break any ice because they're all pals.
correct_substitution: He doesn't have to ease any initial awkwardness because they're all pals.
explanation_correct: To break the ice means to relieve the awkwardness of a first meeting, which is unnecessary among friends.
incorrect_substitution: He doesn't have to deepen the existing awkwardness because they're all pals.
explanation_incorrect: To break the ice means relieving awkwardness, but the sentence describes making it worse.

example: As they rounded the last corner the leaders had the main field breathing down their necks.
correct_substitution: As they rounded the last corner the leaders had the main field pressing closely behind them.
explanation_correct: To breathe down someone's neck means to follow uncomfortably close behind, describing the field's position at the corner.
incorrect_substitution: As they rounded the last corner the leaders had the main field trailing far out of sight behind them.
explanation_incorrect: To breathe down someone's neck means following very close behind, but the sentence places the field a long way back.

example: All he gets are these one-liners and bum steers and cheerful shrugs that may or may not be disingenuous.
correct_substitution: All he gets are these one-liners and misleading pieces of advice and cheerful shrugs that may or may not be disingenuous.
explanation_correct: A bum steer means false or misleading guidance.
incorrect_substitution: All he gets are these one-liners and thoroughly reliable pieces of advice and cheerful shrugs that may or may not be disingenuous.
explanation_incorrect: A bum steer means bad guidance, but the sentence describes dependable advice, which would not be disingenuous.

example: He tossed the bundle of joy to Rex.
correct_substitution: He tossed the newborn baby to Rex.
explanation_correct: A bundle of joy means a new baby, used here with grim incongruity.
incorrect_substitution: He tossed the worn-out old rag to Rex.
explanation_incorrect: A bundle of joy means a baby, but the sentence substitutes a worthless object.

example: But she refused to allow his surliness to burst her bubble of well-being.
correct_substitution: But she refused to allow his surliness to destroy her happy state of well-being.
explanation_correct: To burst someone's bubble means to spoil their happiness or optimism, which she refused to let happen.
incorrect_substitution: But she refused to allow his surliness to strengthen her happy state of well-being.
explanation_incorrect: To burst someone's bubble means spoiling a good mood, but the sentence describes it improving her mood.

example: After the race, the two men met and sensibly buried the hatchet.
correct_substitution: After the race, the two men met and sensibly made peace.
explanation_correct: To bury the hatchet means to end a quarrel and become friendly again, which is what the two men did.
incorrect_substitution: After the race, the two men met and sensibly renewed their quarrel.
explanation_incorrect: To bury the hatchet means ending a dispute, but the sentence describes the dispute being revived.

example: Appeasement caused by blindness was followed by delaying tactics and doublespeak intended to buy time.
correct_substitution: Appeasement caused by blindness was followed by delaying tactics and doublespeak intended to gain a postponement.
explanation_correct: To buy time means to create delay in order to gain more time, which is the purpose of the tactics described.
incorrect_substitution: Appeasement caused by blindness was followed by delaying tactics and doublespeak intended to force an immediate decision.
explanation_incorrect: To buy time means creating delay, but the sentence describes hurrying matters along, which conflicts with the delaying tactics.

example: Mrs Cole isn't one of the worst cases I've seen, by a long chalk.
correct_substitution: Mrs Cole isn't one of the worst cases I've seen, by a very wide margin.
explanation_correct: By a long chalk means by a great degree, emphasising how far from the worst her case is.
incorrect_substitution: Mrs Cole isn't one of the worst cases I've seen, by the narrowest of margins.
explanation_incorrect: By a long chalk means by a large margin, but the sentence reduces it to a tiny difference.

example: He had not told Rory everything, not by a long shot.
correct_substitution: He had not told Rory everything, not by a very wide margin.
explanation_correct: By a long shot means by a great degree, emphasising how much he left unsaid.
incorrect_substitution: He had not told Rory everything, though only by the smallest possible margin.
explanation_incorrect: By a long shot means by a large degree, but the sentence reduces the gap to almost nothing.

example: By and large, the same people are still in positions of power in those authorities.
correct_substitution: In general, the same people are still in positions of power in those authorities.
explanation_correct: By and large means generally speaking or on the whole, qualifying the claim about who holds power.
incorrect_substitution: In one exceptional case only, the same people are still in positions of power in those authorities.
explanation_incorrect: By and large means something is generally true, but the sentence restricts it to a single exception.

example: At times, by dint of heroic effort, the Elves achieved a breathing space and cleared their lands.
correct_substitution: At times, by means of heroic effort, the Elves achieved a breathing space and cleared their lands.
explanation_correct: By dint of means through the force or agency of something, here heroic effort.
incorrect_substitution: At times, in spite of heroic effort, the Elves achieved a breathing space and cleared their lands.
explanation_incorrect: By dint of means because of something, but the sentence makes the effort an obstacle instead.

example: Having heard it so many times, I can recite the poem by heart now.
correct_substitution: Having heard it so many times, I can recite the poem entirely from memory now.
explanation_correct: By heart means from memory without needing the text, which is the result of hearing it so often.
incorrect_substitution: Having heard it so many times, I can recite the poem only while reading from the page now.
explanation_incorrect: By heart means reciting from memory, but the sentence describes needing the written text, which does not follow from repeated hearing.

example: By hook or by crook, football is being called to account for the years of profligacy.
correct_substitution: By whatever means prove necessary, football is being called to account for the years of profligacy.
explanation_correct: By hook or by crook means by any means available, fair or otherwise, describing the determination to hold football to account.
incorrect_substitution: By strictly proper means only, football is being called to account for the years of profligacy.
explanation_incorrect: By hook or by crook means using any means, including improper ones, but the sentence restricts it to legitimate methods.

example: Meanwhile, my interest in classical music was increasing by leaps and bounds.
correct_substitution: Meanwhile, my interest in classical music was increasing extremely rapidly.
explanation_correct: By leaps and bounds means growing very quickly, describing how fast the interest developed.
incorrect_substitution: Meanwhile, my interest in classical music was increasing almost imperceptibly.
explanation_incorrect: By leaps and bounds means rapid growth, but the sentence describes barely noticeable change.

idiom: by no stretch of the imagination
example: Because by no stretch of the imagination would Ven ever come to love her!
correct_substitution: Because under no possible circumstances would Ven ever come to love her!
explanation_correct: By no stretch of the imagination means something is impossible however generously you consider it, emphasising that Ven never would.
incorrect_substitution: Because with only the slightest effort of imagination, Ven would come to love her!
explanation_incorrect: By no stretch of the imagination means something is impossible to imagine, but the sentence presents it as easy to envisage.

example: In truth, Cabernet is beginning to creep in by the back door.
correct_substitution: In truth, Cabernet is beginning to creep in through indirect and unofficial means.
explanation_correct: By the back door means achieved indirectly or without proper approval, describing how Cabernet is spreading.
incorrect_substitution: In truth, Cabernet is beginning to creep in through a formally announced process.
explanation_incorrect: By the back door means arriving indirectly and unofficially, but the sentence describes an open official process, which conflicts with creeping in.

example: But the police had been called so everything had to be done by the book.
correct_substitution: But the police had been called so everything had to be done in strict accordance with the rules.
explanation_correct: By the book means following the official rules exactly, which the presence of the police required.
incorrect_substitution: But the police had been called so everything had to be done however seemed convenient at the time.
explanation_incorrect: By the book means following the rules exactly, but the sentence describes improvising freely, which the police's presence would discourage.

example: Space-time is therefore an extremely stiff medium, and by the same token small-amplitude waves carry large energies.
correct_substitution: Space-time is therefore an extremely stiff medium, and for that same reason small-amplitude waves carry large energies.
explanation_correct: By the same token means that what follows results from the same reasoning just given, linking stiffness to wave energy.
incorrect_substitution: Space-time is therefore an extremely stiff medium, and for a completely unrelated reason small-amplitude waves carry large energies.
explanation_incorrect: By the same token signals that the same reasoning applies, but the sentence severs the connection between the two claims.

example: By the end of the season, Moores' partners called it a day.
correct_substitution: By the end of the season, Moores' partners decided to stop for good.
explanation_correct: To call it a day means to stop doing something, especially for good, which is what the partners decided.
incorrect_substitution: By the end of the season, Moores' partners committed to carrying on indefinitely.
explanation_incorrect: To call it a day means to stop, but the sentence describes a decision to continue.

example: Give us them two back and we'll call it quits.
correct_substitution: Give us them two back and we'll consider the matter settled.
explanation_correct: To call it quits means to agree a debt or dispute is finished, which is the offer being made.
incorrect_substitution: Give us them two back and we'll consider the dispute still wide open.
explanation_incorrect: To call it quits means treating the matter as settled, but the sentence leaves the dispute unresolved, which removes the point of the offer.

example: Whatever power had deranged his senses, its bluff was called when he made contact with her.
correct_substitution: Whatever power had deranged his senses, its empty threat was exposed when he made contact with her.
explanation_correct: To call someone's bluff means to challenge a threat you believe is hollow, forcing it to be proved, which contact achieved.
incorrect_substitution: Whatever power had deranged his senses, its genuine strength was confirmed when he made contact with her.
explanation_incorrect: To call someone's bluff means exposing a threat as empty, but the sentence describes the power proving real.

example: As a Taurean, you work well with others as long as it is you who calls the shots.
correct_substitution: As a Taurean, you work well with others as long as it is you who makes the decisions.
explanation_correct: To call the shots means to be the one in control of decisions, which is the condition described.
incorrect_substitution: As a Taurean, you work well with others as long as it is you who follows their instructions.
explanation_incorrect: To call the shots means being the one in charge, but the sentence describes taking orders from others.

example: How far should he who pays the piper call the tune?
correct_substitution: How far should he who pays the piper decide what happens?
explanation_correct: To call the tune means to be the one who dictates what is done, which is what paying for something is said to entitle you to.
incorrect_substitution: How far should he who pays the piper defer to everyone else's wishes?
explanation_incorrect: To call the tune means dictating what happens, but the sentence describes yielding control to others.

example: Until recently, this combination of carrots and sticks functioned effectively.
correct_substitution: Until recently, this combination of rewards and punishments functioned effectively.
explanation_correct: Carrot and stick refers to using reward and punishment together to motivate, which is the combination described.
incorrect_substitution: Until recently, this policy of offering rewards with no consequences functioned effectively.
explanation_incorrect: Carrot and stick means combining reward with punishment, but the sentence removes the punishment side entirely.

example: But all the time he himself was carrying his own torch for a lost love.
correct_substitution: But all the time he himself was still secretly devoted to a lost love.
explanation_correct: To carry a torch for someone means to go on loving them from afar, describing his lasting attachment.
incorrect_substitution: But all the time he himself was entirely indifferent to a lost love.
explanation_incorrect: To carry a torch means remaining in love with someone, but the sentence describes complete indifference.

example: Just her to carry the can, the prerogative of natural leaders of men.
correct_substitution: Just her to take the blame, the prerogative of natural leaders of men.
explanation_correct: To carry the can means to accept blame for something that went wrong, which falls to her.
incorrect_substitution: Just her to receive the credit, the prerogative of natural leaders of men.
explanation_incorrect: To carry the can means taking the blame, but the sentence describes receiving praise instead.

example: The anti Hunt campaigners believe they have enough to carry the day tomorrow.
correct_substitution: The anti Hunt campaigners believe they have enough to win tomorrow.
explanation_correct: To carry the day means to win or prevail in a contest, which is what the campaigners expect.
incorrect_substitution: The anti Hunt campaigners believe they have enough to lose narrowly tomorrow.
explanation_incorrect: To carry the day means to prevail, but the sentence describes defeat.

example: Or is it that you think so highly of her that you can't bring yourself to cast her pearls before swine?
correct_substitution: Or is it that you think so highly of her that you can't bring yourself to offer something valuable to those unable to appreciate it?
explanation_correct: To cast pearls before swine means to offer something fine to people incapable of valuing it.
incorrect_substitution: Or is it that you think so highly of her that you can't bring yourself to offer something worthless to those who would treasure it?
explanation_incorrect: The idiom means wasting something valuable on the unappreciative, but the sentence reverses both halves.

example: Let he who is without sin cast the first stone, I may be hearing you say.
correct_substitution: Let he who is without sin be the first to accuse, I may be hearing you say.
explanation_correct: To cast the first stone means to be the first to accuse or condemn someone, reserved here for the blameless.
incorrect_substitution: Let he who is without sin be the last to offer forgiveness, I may be hearing you say.
explanation_incorrect: To cast the first stone means being first to condemn, but the sentence turns it into a matter of withholding forgiveness.

example: Q: Cast your mind back: what built that young body of yours?
correct_substitution: Q: Think back to the past: what built that young body of yours?
explanation_correct: To cast your mind back means to recall an earlier time, which is what the question asks the reader to do.
incorrect_substitution: Q: Look ahead to the future: what built that young body of yours?
explanation_incorrect: To cast your mind back means recalling the past, but the sentence directs attention forward, conflicting with asking what already happened.

example: They certainly caught a cold with Preston at the weekend … rather generous in defeat.
correct_substitution: They certainly suffered a costly setback with Preston at the weekend … rather generous in defeat.
explanation_correct: To catch a cold means to suffer a financial or competitive loss, matching the defeat described.
incorrect_substitution: They certainly enjoyed a comfortable triumph with Preston at the weekend … rather generous in defeat.
explanation_incorrect: To catch a cold means suffering a loss, but the sentence describes an easy win, which conflicts with the defeat mentioned.

example: Marcus caught his eye and spread his hands in confusion.
correct_substitution: Marcus attracted his attention and spread his hands in confusion.
explanation_correct: To catch someone's eye means to attract their attention, which Marcus did before gesturing.
incorrect_substitution: Marcus escaped his notice entirely and spread his hands in confusion.
explanation_incorrect: To catch someone's eye means attracting attention, but the sentence describes going unnoticed, which makes the gesture pointless.

example: Before his eyes dull muddy grass turned into soft reflective banks which caught the sun a thousand ways.
correct_substitution: Before his eyes dull muddy grass turned into soft reflective banks which caught the light a thousand ways.
explanation_correct: To catch the sun here means to reflect sunlight, matching the description of the banks becoming reflective.
incorrect_substitution: Before his eyes dull muddy grass turned into soft reflective banks which blocked out all light entirely.
explanation_incorrect: To catch the sun means to reflect sunlight, but the sentence describes light being shut out, contradicting the reflective banks.

example: They're just sitting around in their warm staff-rooms, chewing the fat, while the kids are sent home.
correct_substitution: They're just sitting around in their warm staff-rooms, chatting idly, while the kids are sent home.
explanation_correct: To chew the fat means to talk casually at length.
incorrect_substitution: They're just sitting around in their warm staff-rooms, working intently, while the kids are sent home.
explanation_incorrect: The idiom means idle chat, but the sentence describes hard work, which the complaint contradicts.

example: Standing on a stage in front of hundreds of people was child's play compared to this.
correct_substitution: Standing on a stage in front of hundreds of people was extremely easy compared to this.
explanation_correct: Child's play means something very easy to do, used to show how much harder the present situation is.
incorrect_substitution: Standing on a stage in front of hundreds of people was extraordinarily difficult compared to this.
explanation_incorrect: Child's play means something very easy, but the sentence calls it difficult, which destroys the comparison.

example: It's not a bad idea to chop and change if you get stuck.
correct_substitution: It's not a bad idea to keep switching your approach if you get stuck.
explanation_correct: To chop and change means to keep altering what you are doing, offered here as a remedy for being stuck.
